title: QuillWorks — model evaluation & deployment tradeoffs (hosted/dedicated/private)
summary: Initial discovery to understand QuillWorks requirements for model selection across hosted, dedicated, and private deployments. Focus on context length, multilingual support, tool-calling/function-calling, latency vs cost tradeoffs, and security/compliance needs. Agreed to run a short benchmark and share security docs and pricing.
topics: hosted vs dedicated vs private tradeoffs
next_steps: Redwood to provide SOC2 and security whitepaper and KMS integration notes
Run 48-hour benchmark on QuillWorks sample workload (hosted + dedicated)
Follow-up technical deep-dive to demo tool-calling with customer data connectors
Send preliminary pricing and reserved capacity options

transcript:
Meeting header
Date/Time: 2026-05-23 15:00 PDT
Duration: 54 minutes
Attendees:
  - Jamie Ortega (Redwood AE)
  - Priya Nair (Redwood SE)
  - Evan Lee (QuillWorks, CTO)
  - Marisol Gomez (QuillWorks, Head of ML)
  - Theo Park (QuillWorks, SRE)

Summary: quick discovery to map model choices (open models) to QuillWorks product needs; heavy on context length and multilingual support as well as function/tool calling integration into their platform. Discussed hosted/dedicated/private tradeoffs and next steps for benchmarking.

Topics: model selection, 32k vs 64k context, multilingual inference, tool-calling/function calling, dedicated capacity latency, private VPC constraints, KMS/HSM, SOC2

Transcript body (timestamps approximate):
[00:00] Jamie Ortega: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, we, um, really appreciate you carving out time. Quick intro — I'm Jamie, AE on the Redwood team, and with me is Priya, our solutions engineer. How's everyone doing?
[00:07] Evan Lee: Good thanks, Jamie. Busy week but, uh, excited to dig in. We wanted to get into how you would approach model selection for our use case, and especially how hosted vs dedicated vs private plays with our data and latency needs.
[00:17] Marisol Gomez: Yeah, I'm Marisol. We own the ML roadmap. Quick context — QuillWorks builds an editor that augments legal drafting across multiple languages. So we care a lot about context length (we have large documents), multilingual fidelity (Spanish, Portuguese, German), and ability to call external tools for e.g., document retrieval and statute lookups.
[00:35] Priya Nair: Great, that's super helpful. Two big axes we'll consider — model capability (multilingual, instruction following, tool-calling) and serving constraints (latency SLOs, cost, and data residency). Can you share ballpark traffic and SLOs?
[00:49] Evan Lee: Right now it's early, but our beta has about 40 concurrent active users, peaks to 120. Latency target for interactive features is sub-800ms for short responses, and up to 2s for document summarization. For legal drafting we want deterministic behaviour too — rollout control is important.
[01:07] Marisol Gomez: Also, we frequently pass long user context — sometimes entire sections of contracts. Typical prompt sizes are 8k to 20k tokens, occasionally hitting 30k. We're evaluating whether 32k is enough or we need 64k.
[01:21] Theo Park: From infra side, we have strict data residency for some customers and are SOC2 aligned. We'll need SSO and RBAC integration; for at-rest encryption we already use AWS KMS, and for private/on-prem we may want HSM.
[01:34] Jamie Ortega: Perfect. Sounds like we should consider a mix — hosted to start for speed, dedicated as you scale for predictable latency, and private if you need strict network isolation. For models, open options like Llama-3 family, Mistral mix, and specialized multilingual variants are good fits; we can also fallback to quantized variants to reduce cost.
[01:55] Priya Nair: To add, model context length options map to cost and memory needs — 32k models are common, 64k options exist but cost more and may increase tail latency. We'll show you a quick comparison table in the benchmark plan.
[02:10] Evan Lee: When you say tool-calling, can Redwood trigger external HTTP APIs from the model? We need that to look up statutes and case law and fetch documents.
[02:19] Priya Nair: Yes — we support tool-calling/function-calling patterns. You can register connectors that the runtime calls; we surface structured outputs and have guardrails. For private deployments we can run connectors inside customer VPC if needed.
[02:31] Marisol Gomez: Are there models that natively support tool-calling better? I've seen references to function-token patterns making things jittery.
[02:39] Priya Nair: Tool-calling is mostly an orchestration layer — the model outputs a structured JSON or a signature, and Redwood routes it. Some higher-capability models are better at following the schema; we keep prompt templates and evals to catch regressions.
[02:52] Evan Lee: Ok. Let's talk about multilingual. Our Spanish and Portuguese quality is paramount — okay to use fine-tuned multilingual open models?
[02:59] Jamie Ortega: Absolutely. We maintain a catalog of open models with Redwood-verified perf profiles. For legal spanish/portuguese, models like Mistral 7B chat fine-tuned for multilingual can be strong, but we usually run evals using your prompt examples to pick the model and decide on quantization.
[03:15] Marisol Gomez: We also have regulatory customers in the EU — data residency will matter. If we use hosted Redwood, do you offer region pinning or EU-only hosting?
[03:24] Priya Nair: Yes, hosted offers region pinning and we have EU regions. But for strict residency or audit control, Private (VPC or on-prem) is the option. Dedicated sits in between — dedicated clusters in chosen regions with isolation at the tenant level.
[03:38] Theo Park: For private, how do you handle KMS integration? We need to ensure keys never leave our control.
[03:44] Jamie Ortega: We support customer-managed keys via AWS KMS and HSM integrations. For Private on-prem we can plug into your HSM; for Redwood-hosted we do envelope encryption with customer KMS when required.
[03:56] Evan Lee: Great. Can you do a quick cost/latency sketch — say for a 20k token request on a 32k context model under hosted vs dedicated?
[04:04] Priya Nair: Rough sketch — hosted uses shared capacity so you get bursty cost but usually lower initial spend; latency depends on routing and load but we target SLOs — typical token-level latency numbers vary. Dedicated provides reserved GPU pools — lower tail latency and predictable throughput; unit cost can drop with reserved commit. For exact numbers we'll run a benchmark since your prompt distribution matters.
[04:25] Marisol Gomez: On benchmarks — what inputs do you need from us?
[04:29] Priya Nair: A few representative prompt sets: 1) short interactive prompts, 2) long-document summarization (20k-30k tokens), 3) multilingual question-answer pairs. Also expected concurrency and sample documents. We prefer sanitized real examples.
[04:43] Evan Lee: We can provide those, sanitised. We'll also want to evaluate memory/kv-cache behavior — e.g., repeated re-runs where prefix caching helps.
[04:52] Priya Nair: Good call. Redwood has prefix/KV caching and we can enable it in benchmarks to show cost savings. We'll include scenarios with and without caching.
[05:03] Theo Park: Network requirements — if we go private, we need to know ports, egress, and whether Redwood needs import/export access to our S3.
[05:11] Jamie Ortega: We'll send a private deployment checklist. Typically we ask for VPC peering, or a private link; for data we can integrate via S3 endpoints — we won't pull any data back to public buckets unless configured.
[05:23] Marisol Gomez: On evals, can Redwood run automated quality regression tests after model updates? We need to ensure fidelity doesn't regress on legal accuracy.
[05:31] Priya Nair: Yes — Redwood Optimize has eval hooks and can run your test sets on model rollouts and alert on quality regressions. We can gate canary rollouts with automatic rollback if accuracy dips.
[05:42] Evan Lee: One concern — hallucination on statute citations is a dealbreaker for us. How do you mitigate that with tool-calling?
[05:50] Priya Nair: We use retrieval-augmented generation with provenance and structured citation outputs. Tool-calling can fetch the source text and the runtime can enforce citation formats; we also include evals that score factuality on your reference corpus.
[06:03] Marisol Gomez: How about data retention — do logs or prompts persist in hosted mode? We need to know for compliance.
[06:10] Jamie Ortega: By default hosted stores logs for a period; we have options to disable retention and to purge logs on request. Dedicated and Private give you more control over retention policies and where logs live.
[06:23] Evan Lee: Ok. Switching to model-specific questions — are there notable tradeoffs between Mistral variants and Llama-3 for multilingual legal tasks?
[06:33] Priya Nair: Mistral tends to be strong on multiple languages in smaller parameter counts and is cost-effective; Llama-3 family has larger-context variants and can be tuned more aggressively. For law-specific output, fine-tuning or supervised alignment with your prompts helps a lot. We'll run bench tests on both families.
[06:48] Marisol Gomez: Do you support quantized weights for these models in Dedicated or Private?
[06:52] Jamie Ortega: Yes, our runtime supports multiple quantization profiles. We can recommend per-workload settings in Redwood Optimize — there is a tradeoff between token quality and compute cost, and sometimes we do mixed precision for latency-sensitive flows.
[07:04] Evan Lee: For the benchmark, can we test function-calling integrated with our search index—like retrieving a statute and then asking model to cite and summarize?
[07:12] Priya Nair: Totally. We'll simulate retrieval via a connector pointing to your sample index. We'll showcase structured outputs and a fallback policy if retrieval fails.
[07:21] Theo Park: Any limitations on context when mixing tool-calling with long prompts? Like does the KV cache break when you trigger connectors midstream?
[07:29] Priya Nair: It depends on how you design the prompt flow. We keep KV cache coherent across calls when same session id used; tool-calls that alter prompt state are manageable but we'll show recommended patterns in the deep-dive.
[07:41] Marisol Gomez: Governance — can we restrict which models are available to product teams? We don't want rogue teams spinning up high-cost models.
[07:48] Jamie Ortega: Yes, there is RBAC and per-route/model policy controls in Redwood Console. You can restrict per-team, set quotas, and enforce model whitelist and fallback chains.
[07:59] Evan Lee: Excellent. On pricing — do you have a simple hosted vs dedicated vs private summary we can share with procurement?
[08:06] Jamie Ortega: We'll include a pricing sheet in the follow-up. High-level: hosted is pay-as-you-go, easiest to start; dedicated is committed capacity with discounts; private is licensed and includes deployment support. We'll send typical numbers plus examples for your workload after the benchmark.
[08:20] Marisol Gomez: Ok, next steps?
[08:23] Jamie Ortega: Action items: we'll send the SOC2 and security whitepaper, Priya will share the benchmark plan. Evan, if you can upload the sample prompts and confirm network layout, we'll schedule the 48-hour benchmark. After that we'll meet for a technical deep-dive focused on tool-calling and private deployment checklist.
[08:40] Evan Lee: Sounds good. We'll aim to get the samples up by Wednesday. Any other open questions from your side?
[08:48] Priya Nair: One small thing — do you have specific success metrics for the pilot? E.g., latency p95, hallucination rate under x, or multilingual BLEU-style numbers?
[08:58] Marisol Gomez: Good point — let's target p95 latency under 1.2s for interactive flows, hallucination precision above 95% for citations, and accuracy on multilingual retrieval QAs above 90%. We'll formalize.
[09:11] Jamie Ortega: Great, we'll use those as gating criteria for the pilot. Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the docs and schedule.
[09:19] Evan Lee: Thanks, talk soon.

End of call
